newsitem.title: FINLAND: State selling seen near-term brake for markka rise.
newsitem.headline: State selling seen near-term brake for markka rise.

text.p: A decision on Monday by the Finnish state to buy forex direct in the market to service debt may ease upward pressure on the markka short-term, but longer term its impact will depend on the forces against it, analysts said.

"This is what the new practice is aimed at and it can have some impact," OKOBANK economist Jorma Vanninen told Reuters. "But of course it all depends on how much muscle there actually is against it," he added.
The Bank of Finland's announcement of the planned new system helped the currency off an earlier peak and DEM/FIM rose to 2.9240 by 1625/1425 GMT after briefly ducking below 2.90.
Finland Bank governor Matti Vanhala said the new scheme meant that "some tens of billions (of markka) will appear on the other side of the demand and supply balance on the foreign exchange market".
Under the previous system, the central bank would be buying currency on the market and selling it to the state for debt servicing purposes.

However, Merita Bank analyst Juha Lehtonen said the scheme should not have any impact in the long run since the forex supply-demand balance does not change just because state demand is no longer channelled via the central bank.
"But the state's scheduled currency-flows have attracted a lot of interest today ... and it remains to be seen what the actual impact will be," he said.
The government is due to repay some 30 billion markka of foreign debt and to spend 12 billion markka in coupon payments on foreign currency loans this year.
One economist said the arrangement may increase volatility. "It is a strange arrangement since it can increase market volatility," he said. -- Roland Moller, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 242
